title: Character-SwitchingI & The Pursuit of the Poised Life
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that pursuing an integrated, one-faced life is strategic, not merely moral, because it stops energy being wasted on playing different selves. Drawing on John Wooden's idea of poise in the Pyramid of Success, he defines poise as simply being yourself and so functioning nearer your true ability. He distinguishes harmless code-switching, adjusting dress and register to context, from character-switching, such as caring for students in one period and gossiping about them in the next. Character-switching creeps in almost unconsciously, like cracks in a sidewalk, and he offers reflection questions to help educators name where and when it happens and what excuses they use.
points: Integrity is presented as a time-tested method for conserving energy and performing nearer one's competency, not only a moral duty.
The useful distinction is between code-switching (adapting style to context, which is fine) and character-switching (changing who you are, which erodes trust).
Disintegration happens gradually and unconsciously, so the first step is admitting you struggle with it rather than assuming you are immune.
Examples of public figures whose success was undermined by integrity lapses illustrate that tiny allowed inconsistencies compound over time.
quotes: If we’re to reach our potential, we must pursue the integrated life; we must strive toward being one-faced. Our aim is to be like those integers we learn about in math class: whole numbers, devoid of cunning; what you see is what you get.

Most people think of poise as calm, self-assured dignity; but I call it “just being you.” When we have poise, we’re not acting, faking or pretending. We’re not trying to be something we’re not, nor are we attempting to live up to others’ expectations. Therefore, when we are being who we really are, we’ll have a greater likelihood of functioning nearer our own level of competency.

Of course we’d dress up for the Governor’s Ball. Of course I wear slacks and a tie when I teach and sweatpants if I’m home with my children. The problem isn’t when we code-switch, but when we character-switch.
If one period I’m teaching students I supposedly care about and the next period I’m gossiping about them with other teachers, that’s character-switching.
You don’t go out and decide that you’ll be someone with integrity issues, someone blind to the reality that everyone else sees. You slip into the disintegrated life, the many selves, bit by bit.
First, accept that you struggle here. Second, analyze the problem and relentlessly pursue it’s solution.
When we allow tiny instances of character-switching, they act like cracks in a sidewalk, worsening over time if left unaddressed.
